## ARGUMENT

### I. Plaintiff Cannot Prevail Under § 1983 Without Showing Each Defendant's Personal Participation in the Alleged Constitutional Violation.

Section 1983 creates a remedy against a person who, acting under color of state law, "subjects, or causes to be subjected," another to a deprivation of federal rights. 42 U.S.C. § 1983. The statute imposes liability for a defendant's own conduct. It does not impose liability for the conduct of others. Because "each Government official, his or her title notwithstanding, is only liable for his or her own misconduct," a plaintiff must plead and prove that each defendant, through his or her own actions, violated the Constitution. *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 677 (2009); *see id.* at 676 (rejecting vicarious liability in § 1983 and *Bivens* actions).

The Tenth Circuit has applied this rule consistently. "[P]ersonal participation in the specific constitutional violation complained of is essential." *Foote v. Spiegel*, 118 F.3d 1416, 1423 (10th Cir. 1997). Individual liability under § 1983 therefore "must be based on personal involvement in the alleged constitutional violation." *Id.*; *accord Henry v. Storey*, 658 F.3d 1235, 1241 (10th Cir. 2011); *Trujillo v. Williams*, 465 F.3d 1210, 1227 (10th Cir. 2006). A plaintiff must also show an "affirmative link" between the defendant's conduct and the violation. *Mitchell v. Maynard*, 80 F.3d 1433, 1441 (10th Cir. 1996); *see Serna v. Colo. Dep't of Corr.*, 455 F.3d 1146, 1151 (10th Cir. 2006).

**A. Supervisory status does not supply personal participation.**

Plaintiff cannot rely on a Defendant's title or position. A supervisor is not liable merely because a subordinate violated the Constitution. *Iqbal*, 556 U.S. at 676; *Gallagher v. Shelton*, 587 F.3d 1063, 1069 (10th Cir. 2009). To reach a supervisor, a plaintiff must establish "(1) personal involvement; (2) causation; and (3) state of mind." *Dodds v. Richardson*, 614 F.3d 1185, 1199 (10th Cir. 2010). The plaintiff must show that the supervisor "set in motion a series of events" that the supervisor knew or reasonably should have known would cause a constitutional deprivation. *Id.* at 1195. Alternatively, the plaintiff must show that the supervisor promulgated, created, implemented, or was responsible for a policy that caused the violation while acting with the requisite state of mind. *Id.* at 1199; *see also Brown v. Montoya*, 662 F.3d 1152, 1164–65 (10th Cir. 2011). A generalized responsibility for supervising an agency, a facility, or the persons who committed the challenged acts does not satisfy this standard. *See Fogarty v. Gallegos*, 523 F.3d 1147, 1162 (10th Cir. 2008).

**B. Collective allegations against "Defendants" are insufficient.**

The personal-participation requirement also governs how a plaintiff must plead the claim. A complaint that attributes conduct to "Defendants" as a group does not give each individual fair notice of the basis for the claim against him or her. The Tenth Circuit has stressed that "it is particularly important . . . that the complaint make clear exactly *who* is alleged to have done *what* to *whom*, to provide each individual with fair notice as to the basis of the claims against him or her." *Robbins v. Oklahoma*, 519 F.3d 1242, 1250 (10th Cir. 2008). The court has applied that principle where, as here, individual-capacity defendants invoke qualified immunity. *Pahls v. Thomas*, 718 F.3d 1210, 1225–26 (10th Cir. 2013) (faulting an analysis that lumped defendants together rather than assessing each defendant's own acts). Allegations that fail to distinguish among defendants cannot plausibly show that any particular defendant personally participated in a violation. *Schneider v. City of Grand Junction Police Dep't*, 717 F.3d 760, 767–68 (10th Cir. 2013).

**C. Application.**

Plaintiff's [complaint/evidentiary record] does not identify any act or omission by Defendant [NAME] that caused the alleged deprivation. [Insert record-specific analysis: Defendant was not present for, did not direct, and did not know of the challenged conduct; the pleading rests on Defendant's title or on group allegations.] Because the record does not show Defendant's personal participation, an affirmative causal link, or the requisite state of mind, Plaintiff's § 1983 claim against Defendant fails as a matter of law. This Court should affirm the judgment in Defendant's favor [or reverse and remand with instructions to dismiss].
